title: How to Compare Subscription Plans Properly
description: A repeatable method for comparing subscription tiers - normalize billing periods, weight the features you use, and catch pricing traps.
content:
Subscription pricing is deliberately confusing: mixed billing periods, feature gates across tiers, annual discounts, introductory rates and per-seat scaling all obscure the single number you need — what the plan costs per month for the features you will actually use. Here is a method that cuts through it.

## Step 1: Normalize the billing periods

Before comparing anything, convert every plan to a monthly and annual equivalent:

- Monthly price stays as-is; annual total = monthly × 12.
- Annual price ÷ 12 gives its monthly equivalent.

A $9.99/month plan and an $89/year plan are not comparable as listed. Normalized: $9.99 versus $7.42 — the annual option is about 26% cheaper per month. Do this first; every later step depends on it.

## Step 2: List only features that differentiate

Feature lists are mostly identical padding ("secure cloud", "fast sync"). Extract only the gates that would change your experience: seats, storage limits, quality or resolution tiers, download counts, offline access, support level, API access. If two plans share a feature, it cannot discriminate between them — drop it from the matrix and keep the table short enough to read at once.

Be strict about inclusion: a feature belongs to a plan only if that plan actually includes it. Ambiguous marketing copy ("advanced" versus "premium") needs the plan's own comparison page as arbiter.

## Step 3: Apply your own weights

Not all differentiators matter equally. For a video service you may weight quality tier at 5 and simultaneous screens at 2; for storage, capacity may be everything. Weight 1–5, with only true deal-breakers at 5. The comparison that matters is between plans that pass your threshold features — delete plans missing must-haves before scoring anything.

## Step 4: Read the traps

- **Introductory rates.** First-year discounts that reprice later: compare at the renewal price.
- **Per-seat minimums.** Team plans often bill a minimum seat count; the effective per-seat price depends on your team size.
- **Feature trials.** Higher tiers offered free for 30 days reset to paid — know the end date.
- **Annual lock-in.** Annual savings buy a year of commitment; if cancellation risk is high, price that option into the comparison.
- **Add-on sprawl.** The base plan minus needed add-ons may cost more than the next tier up. Total the add-ons you require, not the sticker.

## Step 5: Decide with margin intact

If the normalized cost difference between your top two candidates is under 5% and feature sets are close, the plans are effectively tied — choose on service quality, cancellation terms or the smaller commitment rather than agonizing over the arithmetic. When the gap is large, check once more that you transcribed the prices correctly, then take the winner.

## Keeping the audit honest

Run this exercise annually. Subscriptions creep: prices rise, tiers change, and plans you once used quietly become muscle memory. Pairing a plan comparison with a full subscription audit — listing every recurring charge against its annual total — usually surfaces both the better plan and the subscriptions worth dropping entirely.
